canonical_statement: The study investigated the association between β-lactam-first versus vancomycin-first administration and mortality in a large multihospital cohort of patients with suspected sepsis.

This was a retrospective cohort study of adults admitted from the emergency department at 5 Mass General Brigham hospitals, including 2 academic and 3 community hospitals, between June 2015 and August 2022.

source_anchor.paragraph: Study Design, Setting, and Data Source

canonical_statement: Eligibility required adults with suspected infection within 24 hours of emergency department arrival plus acute organ dysfunction within 12 hours, with both vancomycin and a qualifying broad-spectrum β-lactam administered within 24 hours.

population.label: Adults with suspected sepsis on admission
inclusion_criteria: Blood culture draw and intravenous antibiotic administration within 24 hours of ED arrival
Acute organ dysfunction within 12 hours of ED arrival
Both a broad-spectrum β-lactam and vancomycin within 24 hours

canonical_statement: The study excluded interhospital transfers, patients with comfort measures or death within 6 hours, psychiatric or obstetric admissions, pre-arrival antibiotics, incomplete key physiologic data, and simultaneous β-lactam/vancomycin starts within 1 minute.

population.label: Study exclusion criteria
exclusion_criteria: Comfort measures or death within 6 hours of arrival
Admission to psychiatry or obstetric services
Incomplete vital signs or missing key labs within 12 hours
First β-lactam and vancomycin infusion start times within 1 minute

canonical_statement: Qualifying acute organ dysfunction included systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg, lactate >2.0 mmol/L, noninvasive or invasive mechanical ventilation, creatinine >2.0 mg/dL with a ≥50% rise from baseline, bilirubin >2.0 mg/dL with a ≥50% rise, or platelets <100,000/μL with a ≥50% fall from baseline.
The exposure of interest was antibiotic sequence: a β-lactam-first strategy versus a vancomycin-first strategy.
The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality.

The primary analysis used inverse probability weighting based on propensity scores and a weighted generalized linear model with logit link and robust sandwich variance estimation to compare in-hospital mortality between antibiotic-sequence groups.

Covariates included demographics, encounter characteristics, selected Elixhauser comorbidities and mortality score, physiologic severity markers, body mass index, infection site, and time from emergency department arrival to first antibiotic infusion.

Prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses examined blood-culture positivity, MRSA-positive clinical cultures, antipseudomonal β-lactam use, shock versus no shock, a stricter shock definition, tighter antibiotic/organ-dysfunction time windows, and propensity-score matching.
The propensity-score-matching sensitivity analysis used one-to-one nearest-neighbor matching without replacement with a caliper width of 0.2 standard deviations.
The final analytic cohort comprised 25,391 patients with suspected sepsis who received both a β-lactam and vancomycin within 24 hours.

Before weighting, the vancomycin-first group tended to be younger and less severely ill, with lower comorbidity burden and less oxygen/vasopressor support, and antibiotic sequence became more β-lactam-first over calendar time.
Urinary infection occurred in 10.3% of the β-lactam-first group and 7.5% of the vancomycin-first group.

canonical_statement: After inverse probability weighting, measured covariates were balanced between antibiotic-sequence groups, with no standardized mean differences greater than 10%.
Crude in-hospital mortality was 13.4% (2,874/21,449) after β-lactam first and 13.6% (538/3,942) after vancomycin first; crude OR 0.98 (95% CI 0.89–1.08; P=.67).

canonical_statement: In the primary inverse-probability-weighted analysis, β-lactam first was associated with lower in-hospital mortality than vancomycin first (adjusted OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80–0.99; P=.046).

canonical_statement: When time-to-first antibiotic was replaced by time-to-first β-lactam in the weighted model, the association was attenuated and not statistically significant (adjusted OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82–1.05; P=.25).

canonical_statement: In the Positive blood cultures subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.8 (95% CI 0.62–1.04).
In the Negative blood cultures subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.91 (95% CI 0.81–1.03).
In the Positive MRSA clinical culture subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.91 (95% CI 0.55–1.51).
In the No positive MRSA clinical culture subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.89 (95% CI 0.8–1).
In the Antipseudomonal β-lactam administered subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.91 (95% CI 0.81–1.02).
In the Sepsis without shock (primary shock definition) subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.8 (95% CI 0.64–0.99).
In the Septic shock (primary shock definition) subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.92 (95% CI 0.81–1.05).
In the Sepsis without shock (strict shock definition) subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.86 (95% CI 0.74–0.995).
In the Septic shock (strict shock definition) subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.95 (95% CI 0.79–1.15).
In the Antibiotics within 12 h / organ dysfunction within 6 h subgroup, the adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality with β-lactam first versus vancomycin first was 0.86 (95% CI 0.77–0.99).

canonical_statement: In the propensity-score-matched sensitivity analysis, 3,938 patients in each sequence group were matched and the mortality estimate remained directionally similar but nonsignificant (adjusted OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.82–1.07).

The authors concluded that β-lactam administration before vancomycin was associated with a modest reduction in the odds of in-hospital mortality in the primary analysis, while secondary analyses were attenuated and nonsignificant.
The authors stated that the findings support prioritizing β-lactam therapy in most patients with sepsis but ideally require confirmation in randomized trials because of residual confounding risk.
The cohort came from 5 hospitals in a single healthcare system, limiting generalizability, especially to regions with different MRSA prevalence.
Not every patient meeting the study definition of suspected sepsis necessarily had a bacterial infection; some may have had viral, fungal, or noninfectious conditions.
The analysis did not account for other sepsis treatments such as volume and timing of fluid resuscitation that could affect the sequence–mortality relationship.
The study could not determine whether delays in β-lactam administration after vancomycin reflected logistical constraints such as limited intravenous access or changes in clinicians’ treatment plans.
Residual confounding remained possible despite detailed adjustment because the study was observational.
